newsitem.title: UK: British money world's "Superwoman" falls to earth.
newsitem.headline: British money world's "Superwoman" falls to earth.

text.p: The resignation of "Superwoman" Nicola Horlick has dragged the obscure world of pension fund management into the spotlight and exposed British schadenfreude at high-flying women who slip up in a man's world.

Horlick, 35, quit her one million pound ($1.67 million) a year job at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management after being suspended from her post amid allegations that she tried to persuade staff members to accompany her to another firm.

Most interestingly for many Britons, it emerged that she had managed to combine her high-pressure job managing billions of pounds of pension fund money with looking after five children, one of whom suffered from leukaemia.

All this, including her luxury London house and her country property, was made more manageable by the fact that her husband Tim also had a lucrative job in banking and the family could afford a small platoon of servants.
But Superwoman was not all efficiency. A meeting with her chief executive on Wednesday in an attempt to sort things out "ended up with me in tears", Horlick told the Financial Times.
Her fall from grace came in a week that two other million-pound-a-year stars also abruptly quit their jobs -- Newcastle United soccer manager Kevin Keegan and top BBC radio disc jockey Chris Evans.

The fate of the three made clear that 1990s Britain places the highest value on the worlds of high finance, showbusiness and football. But the fall of Horlick has evinced a particular fascination because she is a woman.

Dry reports on the financial pages of the newspapers have been accompanied by lifestyle pieces in the features sections wondering whether in the 1990s it is possible for a capable woman to "have it all" -- a top job and a loving family.
The model for this kind of woman was author Shirley Conran, who in her 1970s book "Superwoman" declared that "life is too short to stuff a mushroom".

But Conran recently concluded that even without wasting time on such niceties as mushroom-stuffing, Superwoman status was just too much of an effort, leaving many British women wondering if all their aspirations had been in vain.
Those worries appear to have intensified after the untimely fall of the capable Horlick, described by gossipy colleagues as the "Margaret Thatcher of the pension fund industry".
"The message the rest of us get is that a woman can succeed in a top job only if she is superhuman," said the Guardian newspaper.
"And hence the delighted headlines yesterday that suggested the superheroine who soars above is to be grounded, brought down to earth where she belongs."
The Independent agreed. "You can almost hear the crowing. There she is, Little Miss Have-It-All, finally floored by trying to have too much."
There have been high-flying women in the City of London before but many have not had young families.

What inspired respect for Horlick was the fact that she earned her million pounds while sticking strictly to a 45-hour week -- practically part-time by the standards of many financial dealers -- in order to be with her family.
Horlick has threatened to take legal action against her former employers and even if she fails, she can expect to land another top job.
It is all in stark contrast to the fate of 1,300 workers at car giant Ford, who, on the day Horlick quit, were told they can look forward to life on the dole in Liverpool.
